## Proof

Let $C$ be a smooth projective curve of genus $1$ over $\mathbb{C}$, and let $p, q \in C$. Suppose there is a rational function $f \in \mathbb{C}(C)^\times$ with $(f) = p - q$. We claim $p = q$.

**Key tool: the Abel–Jacobi map on a genus 1 curve.**

Fix a base point $p_0 \in C$. The Abel–Jacobi map
$$\alpha : C \longrightarrow \operatorname{Jac}(C) = \operatorname{Pic}^0(C), \qquad x \longmapsto [x - p_0]$$
sends a point to the linear equivalence class of the degree-zero divisor $x - p_0$. By the classical Abel–Jacobi theory, for a curve of genus $g$ the map $\alpha$ is injective when $g \geq 1$; in particular, for $g = 1$ the map $\alpha$ is an isomorphism of $C$ onto the one-dimensional abelian variety $\operatorname{Jac}(C)$.

(Concretely for $g=1$: $\operatorname{Jac}(C)$ is a one-dimensional complex torus $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$, and $\alpha$ identifies $C$ with this torus via the Weierstrass uniformization; the map is biholomorphic, hence injective.)

**Applying it to the hypothesis.**

The existence of $f$ with $(f) = p - q$ means exactly that the divisor $p - q$ is principal, i.e., linearly equivalent to zero:
$$p - q \sim 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad [p - q] = 0 \in \operatorname{Pic}^0(C).$$

Writing $[p - q] = [p - p_0] - [q - p_0] = \alpha(p) - \alpha(q)$, the condition $[p - q] = 0$ becomes
$$\alpha(p) = \alpha(q).$$

Since $\alpha$ is injective (being an isomorphism for genus $1$), we conclude
$$p = q.$$

**Conclusion.** On a genus $1$ curve, no two distinct points are linearly equivalent: the only principal divisor of the form $p - q$ is the trivial one $p - p$. Hence $p$ must equal $q$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
